text:
**Short answer:** For a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with at least 1,300W of surge output and about 1,000Wh of capacity for part of a day. For a full 24 hours, plan on roughly 1,400-2,000Wh.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts (the most common failure point).** A compressor briefly draws about 2-3x its running watts when it starts. Sources put this at roughly 1,000-1,300W for typical fridges and up to 2,400W for large or older ones. If the station's surge rating is too low, it trips as soon as the fridge starts ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
2. **Continuous watts.** A fridge runs at about 100-250W, so nearly any 1,000W-class station covers this. Add up anything else you'll plug in at the same time.
3. **Watt-hours.** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so average use is far below the running watts. Sources estimate about 41-70Wh per hour, or roughly 1,000-1,400Wh per day including inverter losses and a safety margin ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator), [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).

Also make sure the inverter is **pure sine wave**, since modified sine wave can make compressors run hot or fail to start.

## Rough sizing guide

| Outage length | Capacity to look for |
|---|---|
| ~12-17 hours | ~1,000Wh |
| ~24 hours | ~1,400-2,000Wh |
| 2 days | ~2,800Wh+ |
| 3 days | ~4,200Wh+ |

The same sources estimate that a ~1,070Wh Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 runs a fridge about 17 hours, and a ~2,000Wh unit about 33 hours ([HomeGrid HQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).

## Make it more precise

- Use your fridge's EnergyGuide label: kWh per year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts. A large side-by-side with an ice maker can average about double a typical efficient model ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- Runtime ≈ rated Wh × 0.85 ÷ average watts. For example, 1,600Wh × 0.85 ÷ 70W ≈ 19 hours ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)).
- Keep the door shut. HomeGrid HQ cites the USDA's guidance that food is unsafe after 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed.

## Models that fit

- **BLUETTI AC180** (1,152Wh, 1,800W, 2,700W peak) is a good fit for part of a day. It's the top pick in the [BlackBox Supplies guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), listed at about $399-699 recently.
- **Jackery Explorer 1000 v2** (~1,070Wh) is also in that [guide](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), at about $449-799 recently.
- **Anker SOLIX S2000** (2,010Wh, 1,500W, 3,000W peak) is aimed at a full day. See it on [Anker's page](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator), where it's listed at $699.99 after coupon. This is Anker's own marketing, so treat its claims accordingly.
- **BLUETTI AC200L** (2,048Wh, 2,400W, expandable to 8,192Wh) suits you if you might add capacity for multi-day outages.
